question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot 3 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{6},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is 

$$
m={f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})=0.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
